section.title: The Passover
section.sectionRationale: This is the founding ordinance of Israel's national life, instituted on the very night of deliverance and commanded to be kept forever. It gives Israel, and the whole Bible after it, its central picture of judgment averted by a substitute's blood.
section.thesis: The LORD institutes the Passover: a spotless lamb slain in the place of the firstborn, its blood marking the door so that judgment passes over, to be kept as a perpetual memorial of redemption.
section.frameNote: Four movements: instructions for choosing and eating the lamb; the promise that the blood will avert judgment; the memorial feast for the generations to come; and Moses relaying it all to the elders, who believe and obey.

units.label: Instructions for the lamb
units.note: a new calendar, a chosen lamb

media.alt: A spotless lamb and blood on a doorframe
media.caption: A lamb without blemish, its blood marking the door.

verses.text: Now the LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt,
“This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year.
Tell the whole congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month each man must select a lamb for his family, one per household.
If the household is too small for a whole lamb, they are to share with the nearest neighbor based on the number of people, and apportion the lamb accordingly.
Your lamb must be an {{unblemished|unblemished}} year-old male, and you may take it from the sheep or the goats.
You must keep it until the fourteenth day of the month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel will slaughter the animals at twilight.
They are to take some of the {{blood|blood}} and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs.
They are to eat the meat that night, roasted over the fire, along with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Do not eat any of the meat raw or cooked in boiling water, but only roasted over the fire, its head and legs and inner parts.
Do not leave any of it until morning; before the morning you must burn up any part that is left over.
This is how you are to eat it: You must be fully dressed for travel, with your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD's {{passover|Passover}}.

units.label: The judgment and the sign of blood
units.note: the blood shall be a sign, and I will pass over you

verses.text: On that night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn male, both man and beast, and I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD.
The blood on the houses where you are staying will distinguish them; when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.
And this day will be a memorial for you, and you are to celebrate it as a feast to the LORD, as a permanent statute for the generations to come.

For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. On the first day you are to remove the leaven from your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened from the first day through the seventh must be cut off from Israel.
On the first day you are to hold a sacred assembly, and another on the seventh day. You must not do any work on those days, except to prepare the meals, that is all you may do.
So you are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt. You must keep this day as a permanent statute for the generations to come.
In the first month you are to eat unleavened bread, from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day.

For seven days there must be no leaven found in your houses. If anyone eats something leavened, that person, whether a foreigner or native of the land, must be cut off from the congregation of Israel.
You are not to eat anything leavened; eat unleavened bread in all your homes.”
Then Moses summoned all the elders of Israel and told them, “Go at once and select for yourselves a lamb for each family, and slaughter the Passover lamb.
Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin, and brush the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe. None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning.

When the LORD passes through to strike down the Egyptians, He will see the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe and will pass over that doorway; so He will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses and strike you down.
And you are to keep this command as a permanent statute for you and your descendants.
When you enter the land that the LORD will give you as He promised, you are to keep this service.
When your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’

you are to reply, ‘It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt when He struck down the Egyptians and spared our homes.’” 
Then the people bowed down and worshiped.
And the Israelites went and did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.

unblemished.gloss: Without defect, whole, complete. The lamb must be flawless, fit to stand in another's place; the New Testament calls Christ a lamb without blemish or defect, 1 Peter 1:19.

blood.gloss: Blood, the life poured out. It is not the lamb's death alone that saves but the blood applied, visibly marking the house; the same principle runs through the whole sacrificial system and into the cross.

passover.gloss: To pass over, to spring over, to spare. The word names both the act, God passing over the marked houses, and the festival that remembers it, and gives its name to Christ, our Passover lamb, 1 Corinthians 5:7.

basic.context: On the very last night in Egypt, God gives Israel a new calendar and a new meal. Each family takes a spotless lamb, kills it, and paints its blood on the doorframe. That night, judgment falls on Egypt's firstborn, but wherever the blood is seen, the LORD passes over the house.
basic.hermeneutics: This really happened, on a specific night, and Israel was commanded to keep it every year after. It teaches an unchanging truth: judgment is real, and only a substitute's blood, not personal goodness, turns it aside. Christians do not keep the Passover meal itself, but the substance it pictured is fulfilled in Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: The lamb must be tamim, without blemish, a flawless substitute. What saves is the dam, the blood, applied and seen, not simply the animal's death in the abstract. And the name pesach, Passover, describes exactly what happens: the LORD springs over, passes over, the marked house.
basic.typology: This is the Bible's clearest picture of substitutionary atonement before the cross: an unblemished lamb dies so the firstborn lives, and its blood, applied by faith, is what saves. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb outright; John's Gospel deliberately echoes Passover details in Jesus' death.
basic.christ: 1 Corinthians 5:7 names Jesus directly as our Passover lamb, sacrificed once for all. John notes that none of Jesus' bones were broken, fulfilling the Passover rule in Exodus 12:46, and John the Baptist calls Him the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
basic.god: God is the one who judges Egypt, yet He is also the one who provides the way of escape before He strikes. His justice and His mercy meet exactly at the doorframe: judgment is real and falls, but a substitute has already borne it for those who trust and obey.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 5:7 calls Christ our Passover lamb. John 19:36 sees the unbroken bones fulfilled at the cross. John 1:29 calls Jesus the Lamb of God. 1 Peter 1:18-19 speaks of redemption by the precious blood of a lamb without blemish or defect.
basic.oneStory: This is the night Israel learns the shape of salvation: not escape by good behavior, but rescue through a substitute's blood, applied in faith and obedience. Every Passover after this one points forward to the true Lamb, until Christ dies at Passover itself and becomes what this night only pictured.

context.literary:
Exodus 12:1-28 interrupts the story at its most dramatic point. Chapter 11 has announced the final plague and ended with Moses leaving Pharaoh 'hot with anger,' Exodus 11:8. The reader expects the blow to fall at once. Instead the narrative stops and gives two long speeches of instruction, the LORD's to Moses and Aaron in verses 1 to 20, then Moses' to the elders in verses 21 to 27, before the plague finally strikes in verse 29. The pause is the point. Before Israel is delivered it is taught how to be delivered and how to remember it, so that the liturgy is built into the event itself.

The first speech moves in a careful order: a new calendar, verse 2; the choosing and keeping of the lamb, verses 3 to 6; the blood and the meal, verses 7 to 11; the divine explanation, verses 12 and 13; and then the seven days of unleavened bread, verses 14 to 20. The explanation in verses 12 and 13 is the hinge, and it is built on a stark contrast. 'I will pass through' and 'I will strike' stand against 'I will pass over' and 'No plague will fall on you.' The same night, the same God, two outcomes, and the only thing that separates them is the blood.

The second speech is not a copy of the first. Moses adds the hyssop and the basin, verse 22, the command to stay indoors until morning, and the destroyer who will not be allowed in, verse 23. He also looks past the night itself to the land, verse 25, and to the questions of children, verse 26. The unit closes with two short notes of response: worship in verse 27 and obedience in verse 28, 'just what the LORD had commanded.' That phrase becomes a refrain of the book and returns in the building of the tabernacle, Exodus 39:32 and 40:16.
context.historical:
The instructions assume ordinary households in Goshen, not a temple or priesthood. There is as yet no altar, no Levite, no tabernacle. Each father acts as the priest of his house, choosing the animal, slaughtering it, and applying the blood. The word the BSB renders 'lamb' can mean a lamb or a kid, as the footnote to verse 3 notes, which is why verse 5 allows the animal to come 'from the sheep or the goats.' A yearling male was the prime of the flock, an animal of real value to a family of shepherds.

The timing is precise. The animal is set apart on the tenth day and kept until the fourteenth, and it is killed 'at twilight,' literally 'between the two evenings,' the same phrase used later for the daily evening lamb at the tabernacle, Exodus 29:39. The month is later called Abib, the month of the ripening barley, Exodus 13:4 and 23:15, falling in the spring. Verse 2 makes it the head of Israel's year. Their calendar would begin not with a harvest or a king's accession but with the night of their rescue.

The meal itself was a meal for travellers. Roasting whole over the fire needed no pots and could be done quickly; the bread had no time to rise; the diners ate with their robes tucked into their belts, sandals on and staff in hand, verse 11. The bitter herbs recalled lives made 'bitter with hard labor,' Exodus 1:14.

Later practice adapted but did not abandon these details. Deuteronomy 16:2-6 moves the slaughter to 'the place the LORD will choose.' Israel kept the Passover at Sinai, Numbers 9:1-5, on entering the land at Gilgal, Joshua 5:10, and in the great reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah, 2 Chronicles 30 and 35, and the returned exiles kept it at the rebuilt temple, Ezra 6:19-22. By the time of Jesus the lambs were slaughtered at the temple and eaten in households across Jerusalem.
context.canonical:
The Passover never stays in Exodus. The law restates it in Leviticus 23:5-8, Numbers 9 and 28:16-25, and Deuteronomy 16:1-8. Numbers 9:6-14 adds a second Passover a month later for those who were unclean or away on a journey, a small window into how seriously Israel took the command that no one should miss it. The historical books mark Israel's moments of renewal by it: Gilgal, Joshua 5:10-11, where the manna stops the next day; Hezekiah's invitation to the northern tribes, 2 Chronicles 30:1; Josiah's Passover, of which 2 Kings 23:22 says 'no such Passover had been observed from the days of the judges'; and the first Passover after the exile, Ezra 6:19-21.

The poets and prophets take up its language. Psalm 78:51, 105:36 and 136:10 sing of the firstborn struck down, the last setting it within the refrain of God's 'loving devotion.' Isaiah 31:5 uses the verb of Passover for the LORD's protection of Jerusalem: 'He will pass over it and preserve it.' Isaiah 52:12 promises a second exodus that will not be in haste, reversing the hurried meal of Exodus 12:11. Ezekiel 9:4-6 pictures a mark set on the faithful before judgment passes through Jerusalem, a clear echo of the marked doors.

In the New Testament the Passover frames the life and death of Jesus. Luke 2:41 shows His family going up to Jerusalem for it every year. John structures his Gospel around successive Passovers, John 2:13, 6:4 and 11:55. The Synoptic Gospels present the Last Supper as a Passover meal, Mark 14:12 and Luke 22:15, and John sets the crucifixion on 'the day of Preparation for the Passover,' John 19:14. Paul writes 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and draws out the leaven as a moral lesson in the next verse. Hebrews 11:28 treats Moses' keeping of the Passover as an act of faith, and Revelation's Lamb 'who appeared to have been slain,' Revelation 5:6, gathers the whole pattern into one figure.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand that their freedom began with a meal eaten under the shadow of death. They were not spared because they were Israelites by birth alone; verse 13 makes the blood, not the bloodline, the thing that distinguishes the houses, and an Israelite who ignored the command would have had no promise of protection. In the earlier plagues the LORD Himself had made the distinction between Goshen and Egypt, Exodus 8:22-23 and 9:4. Now, for the first time, Israel has something to do, and what it does is to shelter under a provision God has appointed.

He also meant them to grasp that the night belonged to the LORD. It is 'the LORD's Passover,' verse 11, and 'a feast to the LORD,' verse 14. The judgment on Egypt's gods in verse 12 tells Israel that the powers they had lived under for generations were nothing before Him.

And he wanted a people who would remember by doing. The calendar, the week of bread without leaven, the annual question of children, all of it was designed so that later generations who had never seen Egypt would say, as verse 27 puts it, that the LORD 'spared our homes.' Obedience and worship close the passage because that is the response the whole speech was meant to produce.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is prescriptive for Israel. It commands a feast 'as a permanent statute for the generations to come,' verses 14, 17 and 24, and Israel was bound to keep it. Some elements were for that first night only: the blood on the doorposts, eating with staff in hand, staying indoors until morning. Later Passovers moved the slaughter to the sanctuary, Deuteronomy 16:5-6, and there is no record that later generations painted their doorframes.

For Christians the command is read through its fulfilment. The New Testament never tells the church to keep the Passover as Israel did, but it does tell believers to 'keep the feast' with 'the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth,' 1 Corinthians 5:8. What carries over is the substance: shelter under the blood of Christ, a life cleared of the old leaven, a table that remembers, 1 Corinthians 11:24-26, and readiness to travel, for believers are also told to 'prepare your minds for action,' 1 Peter 1:13. The permanence of the statute is honoured not by repeating the shadow but by holding to the reality.

debates.question: Should Christians keep a Passover meal today?

views.label: Fulfilled, not repeated
views.case: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed, 1 Corinthians 5:7. Hebrews argues that the shadows of the law give way to the reality in Christ, Hebrews 10:1, and the meal He gave His church on Passover night is the Lord's Supper, 1 Corinthians 11:23-26. On this view a ritual re-enactment adds nothing and may blur the newness of the new covenant.

views.label: Instructive remembrance
views.case: Some Christians hold a Christian seder as a teaching occasion, to understand the setting of the Last Supper and the Jewish roots of the gospel. They do not treat it as binding, and they are careful to distinguish it from the Lord's Supper, but they see value in children asking, as verse 26 anticipates, what the service means.

debates.bearing: Neither view makes the Passover obligatory, since Paul warns against being judged over feasts that were 'a shadow of the things to come,' Colossians 2:16-17. The real question is whether a teaching meal helps believers see Christ more clearly without replacing the table He appointed.

debates.question: What does the verb 'pass over' mean in verses 13 and 23?

views.label: To skip or pass by
views.case: The same root describes limping or hopping in 1 Kings 18:21 and 18:26 and becoming lame in 2 Samuel 4:4. On this reading the LORD moves through the land striking house after house and leaps over those marked with blood. It fits the contrast of verse 12, 'I will pass through,' and has shaped the English name of the feast.

views.label: To stand guard over
views.case: Isaiah 31:5 uses the verb in parallel with shield, deliver and preserve: 'He will pass over it and preserve it.' Verse 23 also distinguishes the LORD from 'the destroyer' whom He 'will not allow' to enter. On this reading the LORD does not merely skip the house; He stands at its door and protects those inside.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not far apart, and both keep the point that the LORD Himself decides who is spared. The protective sense deepens the picture: the blood does not hide Israel from God; it places them under His guard.

debates.question: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal?

views.label: Yes, on Passover night
views.case: Matthew, Mark and Luke all present the meal as the Passover, Mark 14:12 and Luke 22:15, with Jesus saying He had 'eagerly desired to eat this Passover.' The bread and cup take on new meaning within that setting.

views.label: The day before, with Jesus dying as the lambs were killed
views.case: John places the trial before the Jewish leaders had eaten the Passover, John 18:28, and the crucifixion on 'the day of Preparation for the Passover,' John 19:14. Some conclude that John presents Jesus dying at the hour of the Passover sacrifice.

debates.bearing: Several harmonisations have been proposed, including different calendars in use or John's 'Preparation' referring to the Passover week. Whatever the solution, all four Gospels agree that Jesus died at Passover and interpreted His death by it.

study.originalLanguages:
The animal of verse 3 is a seh, a word for a single head of the flock that covers both lambs and young goats, as the BSB footnote explains. It is the word Isaac uses on Mount Moriah, 'where is the lamb for the burnt offering?' Genesis 22:7, and Abraham's answer, 'God Himself will provide the lamb,' Genesis 22:8. The Passover is the first time Israel as a whole is told to take such a seh, and the echo of Moriah is hard to miss.

Tamim in verse 5 means whole, complete, without defect. It is used of animals fit for sacrifice, Leviticus 22:21, but also of people and of God. Noah was 'blameless in his generation,' Genesis 6:9; Abram was told, 'walk before Me and be blameless,' Genesis 17:1; and 'as for God, His way is perfect,' Psalm 18:30. The word joins the soundness of the offering to the integrity God looks for in His people.

The time of slaughter in verse 6 is bein ha'arbayim, literally 'between the two evenings,' as the footnote notes, usually taken as the span between sunset and dark. The same phrase fixes the evening lamb of the daily offering, Exodus 29:39, and the quail in the wilderness, Exodus 16:12.

The blood is to go on the mezuzot, the two doorposts, and the mashqof, the lintel, as the footnote to verse 7 says. The doorposts reappear in Deuteronomy 6:9, 'Write them on the doorposts of your houses,' the word that later gave its name to the small case fixed to Jewish doorframes. The doorway that once bore the blood would later bear the word. In verse 22 the 'basin' is saf, which elsewhere means a threshold, as in Judges 19:27, and some interpreters think the blood was caught at the foot of the door, so that the whole doorway was framed in it.

The name pesach comes from the verb pasach. Elsewhere the root describes a limping or unsteady gait, 1 Kings 18:21 and 2 Samuel 4:4, while Isaiah 31:5 uses it for the LORD shielding Jerusalem. Verse 13 turns the verb into a promise and verse 27 into a confession: the LORD 'passed over the houses.'

Two further words carry the theology. The blood is an ot, a 'sign,' verse 13, the word used for the rainbow, Genesis 9:13, and for circumcision, Genesis 17:11. And the destroyer of verse 23 is the mashchit, the participle of the verb 'to destroy' already used in verse 13, 'no plague will fall on you to destroy you.' The same word describes the angel 'who was destroying the people' in 2 Samuel 24:16. Hebrews 11:28 calls him 'the destroyer of the firstborn.'

Finally, the 'service' of verses 25 and 26 is avodah, the same noun used in Exodus 1:14 for the harsh labour imposed by Egypt. Israel moves from avodah for Pharaoh to avodah for the LORD, from forced labour to worship, which is exactly what Moses had demanded, 'let My son go so that he may worship Me,' Exodus 4:23.

typology.type: The lamb chosen, kept and slain, Exodus 12:3-6
typology.fulfillment: The lamb was set apart on the tenth day and watched for four days before it died, and it had to be whole and in its prime. Jesus is announced by John as 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, and Peter says believers were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. The escalation is that this Lamb is examined and found faultless in His whole life, not only in body, Hebrews 9:14. The type falls short because the Passover lamb had to be killed again every year, while Christ offered Himself once, Hebrews 10:4 and 10:10.

typology.type: The blood on the doorway, Exodus 12:7 and 12:13
typology.fulfillment: Blood applied to each household was the one thing that turned judgment aside, and the protection extended to everyone who stayed inside. The New Testament speaks of believers 'justified by His blood' and therefore 'saved from wrath through Him,' Romans 5:9, and of Jesus as the one who rescues 'from the coming wrath,' 1 Thessalonians 1:10. Hebrews speaks of 'the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel,' Hebrews 12:24. The type falls short because the Passover blood marked wood and protected for a night; Christ's blood cleanses the conscience and the person, 1 John 1:7.

The lamb was roasted whole and eaten without breaking a bone, the rule repeated in Exodus 12:46 and Numbers 9:12. John records that the soldiers broke the legs of the men crucified with Jesus but not His, and then says, 'these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: Not one of His bones will be broken,' John 19:36. The correspondence is small in itself but deliberate, since John has already set the crucifixion at Passover, John 19:14, and mentions the hyssop at the cross, John 19:29. The detail marks Jesus as the true lamb of the feast.

For seven days leaven was removed from every Israelite house, and whoever ate it was cut off. Paul reads the week as a picture of the Christian life that flows from the sacrifice: 'Get rid of the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. The order matters. The lamb dies first and the house is then cleansed; holiness follows redemption rather than earning it. The type falls short because Israel's cleansing was outward and temporary, while believers are called to put away malice and wickedness from the heart, 1 Corinthians 5:8.

typology.type: The meal eaten in haste by travellers, Exodus 12:11
typology.fulfillment: Israel ate dressed for the road, because the meal was the start of a journey out of bondage. At the Transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about 'His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:31, where the Greek word is exodos. The church that eats His meal is also a pilgrim people, told to be 'dressed for service' with lamps burning, Luke 12:35, proclaiming the Lord's death 'until He comes,' 1 Corinthians 11:26. The type reaches its end at 'the marriage supper of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:9, a meal eaten at last with no need for haste.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the calendar of His death. Jesus did not die at a random time. He went up to Jerusalem at Passover, told His disciples 'I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering,' Luke 22:15, and died while the city was keeping the feast. Mark notes that the supper took place 'when the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed,' Mark 14:12, and John dates the crucifixion to 'the day of Preparation for the Passover,' John 19:14. The timing was chosen, and it tells us how Jesus wanted His death understood.

It leads to Christ by the words He spoke over the meal. Taking the bread, He said, 'This is My body, given for you,' and taking the cup, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you,' Luke 22:19-20. At a meal that remembered a lamb whose blood protected households, Jesus pointed to His own body and blood. Matthew adds 'for the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28, which goes beyond anything the first Passover claimed. The Exodus lamb averted a single judgment; Christ's blood deals with the sin that makes judgment necessary. Jesus also said He would not eat it again 'until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God,' Luke 22:16, so the Passover now looks forward as well as back.

It leads to Christ by John's careful details. John the Baptist twice calls Him 'the Lamb of God,' John 1:29 and 1:36. At the cross a sponge is lifted to Him on 'a stalk of hyssop,' John 19:29, the plant Moses told Israel to dip in the blood, Exodus 12:22. His legs are not broken, and John cites the Scripture, 'Not one of His bones will be broken,' John 19:36.

It leads to Christ through Paul's plain statement, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and Peter's 'lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. Revelation completes the thread with a Lamb 'who appeared to have been slain,' whose blood 'purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' Revelation 5:9. The Passover redeemed one nation from one oppressor; the Lamb redeems a people from every nation.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The New Testament does not ask us to find Christ in every detail, the bitter herbs, the staff, the roasting fire. The links above are the ones the apostles themselves make. And there is a contrast as well as a likeness. In Egypt the firstborn of Israel lived because a lamb died in his place. At the cross the firstborn Son of God, Colossians 1:15, was Himself the one who died, and no one passed over Him. The judgment Israel escaped, He bore.
study.god:
The chapter first shows God as the Lord of time. 'This month is the beginning of months for you,' verse 2. Before He brings Israel out of Egypt He reorders their year around His act of rescue. Egypt measured its years by its kings; Israel would measure its year by the night the LORD delivered it. God claims not only the people but the shape of their days.

It shows Him as the only God. 'I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD,' verse 12. Numbers 33:4 looks back on the same night: 'the LORD had executed judgment against their gods.' The plague falls on the firstborn of Pharaoh, whom Egypt regarded as divine, and on the firstborn of the livestock, some of which were sacred in Egyptian religion. The LORD does not compete with the gods of Egypt as one power among many. He judges them.

It shows Him as a God who distinguishes. He had made a distinction in the plagues, Exodus 8:23 and 11:7, but here the distinction runs through a single act. The same God passes through and passes over. Judgment and mercy are not two gods, nor one God in two moods, but one purpose, and the difference between them lies not in the worth of the people but in the provision God appoints. Israel was not less guilty than Egypt; its firstborn were equally under the sentence of verse 12. The blood was God's own answer to that sentence.

It shows Him as the one who both judges and protects. Verse 23 speaks of the LORD passing through and of the destroyer, and it is the LORD who 'will not allow the destroyer' to enter. The judge of Egypt stands guard at Israel's doors. This holds together what we are tempted to separate: God is the one we need to be saved from, and God is the one who saves us.

It shows Him as a God who wants to be remembered and understood. He does not simply act; He explains, and He commands the explanation to be passed on. He expects children to ask, verse 26, and He gives parents the answer. Faith in this God is historical and teachable, tied to what He has done.

For worship, verse 27 gives the right response. When the elders heard these words 'the people bowed down and worshiped,' before a single firstborn had died and before they had left Egypt. They worshiped on the strength of the promise. That is still the posture of faith: to take God at His word about the blood and to bow before Him while the night is still dark.

crossReferences.note: The announcement that stands behind this chapter. At about midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's to the servant girl's, but 'not even a dog will snarl' at Israel, so that Egypt will know 'the LORD makes a distinction.' Exodus 12 explains how that distinction will be made: by the blood on the door.

Isaac asks where the lamb is, and Abraham answers, 'God Himself will provide the lamb.' The same word for a lamb of the flock appears in Exodus 12:3. On Moriah a ram died in place of a son; in Egypt a lamb dies in place of every firstborn son, and the question of the lamb God will provide keeps moving forward.

The LORD will protect Jerusalem like birds hovering overhead: 'He will shield it and deliver it; He will pass over it and preserve it.' Isaiah takes the verb of the Passover and pairs it with shielding and preserving, which supports reading Exodus 12:13 and 12:23 as the LORD standing guard over the marked houses.

Moses restates the feast for life in the land. The month is Abib, the sacrifice is to be offered where the LORD will choose, and the unleavened bread is named 'the bread of affliction, because you left the land of Egypt in haste.' The haste of Exodus 12:11 becomes the lasting meaning of the bread.

Jesus eats the Passover with His disciples and reinterprets it around Himself. The bread is His body given for them, the cup is 'the new covenant in My blood,' and He will not eat it again 'until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.' The memorial of Exodus 12:14 now remembers Him.

The soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus, but finding Him already dead they do not break His. John cites Scripture, 'Not one of His bones will be broken,' echoing Exodus 12:46, and adds that blood and water flowed from His side. The Passover rule is kept at the cross.

Paul applies the week of unleavened bread to a church tolerating sin. A little leaven works through the whole batch, so the old leaven must go, because 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.' The order of Exodus 12, the lamb first and then the clearing of leaven, becomes the order of Christian holiness.

Moses 'kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood' by faith, 'so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel's own firstborn.' Hebrews treats the obedience of Exodus 12:28 as trust in a promise not yet seen, and names the destroyer of Exodus 12:23.

Believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.' Peter joins the Passover lamb's requirement of Exodus 12:5 to the language of redemption from an empty inherited way of life, a new exodus from a different bondage.

Before judgment passes through Jerusalem, a mark is placed on the foreheads of those who grieve over its sins, and the executioners are told not to go near anyone who has the mark. The pattern of Exodus 12:13 returns, but now it falls on Israel itself, and the mark belongs to the repentant rather than to a nation.

John sees 'a Lamb who appeared to have been slain' at the centre of the throne, and the new song praises Him because by His blood He 'purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.' The Passover lamb of one people becomes the Lamb of the whole redeemed world.

Israel's first Passover in the land is kept at Gilgal on the fourteenth day of the month, and the next day they eat the produce of Canaan and the manna stops. Exodus 12:25 had said the service would be kept 'when you enter the land,' and here the promise and the command meet.

study.oneStory:
Genesis ended with a promise and a coffin. Joseph died in Egypt saying 'God will surely attend to you,' Genesis 50:24-25, and Exodus opened with Abraham's children multiplied but enslaved. The Passover is where God's long attention turns into action. Genesis 15:13-14 had told Abraham that his offspring would be strangers in a land not their own and that God would judge the nation they served. Exodus 12 is that judgment and that release.

It also answers something older. Since Genesis 3 humanity has lived under the sentence of death, and the firstborn of every nation stood as much under judgment as anyone. Egypt's firstborn are not uniquely wicked, and Israel's are not uniquely good. What the Passover reveals is the shape of God's remedy: death is not ignored, it is met by a substitute God provides, and those who shelter under its blood live.

The pattern then runs through the whole of Israel's life. The firstborn are claimed by God and redeemed, Exodus 13:2 and 13:13. The tabernacle and its sacrifices grow out of the same logic of blood and atonement. The feast is kept at every turning point of the nation's history, and the prophets reach for its language when they promise a greater exodus to come, Isaiah 52:12. Yet the lambs had to die again every year, and Israel kept falling back into bondage of other kinds. The feast pointed beyond itself.

In the Gospels the pattern comes to rest in Jesus. He dies at Passover as the Lamb of God, and His people are redeemed not from Pharaoh but from sin and death, Colossians 1:13-14. The meal He gives the church is a Passover remembered and transformed, eaten 'until He comes,' 1 Corinthians 11:26.

The story ends at another table. Isaiah promised a feast on God's mountain 'for all the peoples,' when 'He will swallow up death forever,' Isaiah 25:6-8. Revelation calls it 'the marriage supper of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:9. The first Passover was eaten in haste, in the dark, with death at the door. The last will be eaten in the light of God's presence, with no destroyer anywhere and nothing left to flee, because the Lamb who was slain has made all things new.

sermon.title: The Story of the Lamb
sermon.why: Preached on Exodus 12:1-13, Keller works through the Passover lamb as the pattern the whole Bible uses to explain substitutionary atonement, tracing it directly to Christ as the true Lamb of God.

quiz.q: What kind of lamb did each household have to select?

options.text: An unblemished, year-old male, from the sheep or the goats.
options.note: Verse 5 gives this exact requirement, a flawless substitute.

options.text: Any lamb available, blemished or not.
options.note: The text is specific: it must be without blemish, not just any lamb.

options.text: A lamb over three years old.
options.note: The requirement is a year-old male, not an older animal.

options.text: No animal at all was required.
options.note: An animal sacrifice, a lamb or goat, was explicitly required.

quiz.q: What made the difference between judgment and safety on that night?

options.text: The blood applied visibly to the doorframe of the house.
options.note: Verses 13 and 23 make this the deciding sign, seen by the LORD Himself.

options.text: How sincerely the family prayed that night.
options.note: Sincerity mattered, but the text points to the visible blood as the actual sign of safety.

options.text: Whether the family was wealthy enough to buy a large lamb.
options.note: Poorer households could share a lamb; wealth was never the deciding factor.

options.text: Nothing distinguished Israelite and Egyptian homes.
options.note: The text is explicit that the blood made a clear, life-saving distinction.

quiz.q: How were the Israelites to eat the Passover meal, according to verse 11?

options.text: Fully dressed for travel, sandals on, staff in hand, eating in haste.
options.note: This detail signals urgency, they were about to be driven out that very night.

options.text: Reclining at leisure over several days.
options.note: The instructions stress urgency and readiness to leave, not leisure.

options.text: Fasting completely through the night.
options.note: They were commanded to eat the lamb, not fast from it.

options.text: Standing outside the house in the open street.
options.note: They were to stay inside the house until morning, verse 22.

quiz.q: Why was this day to be kept as a permanent statute?

options.text: As a memorial of the LORD bringing Israel's divisions out of Egypt on that very day.
options.note: Verses 14 and 17 give exactly this reason, a remembrance of redemption.

options.text: Because Pharaoh requested an annual tribute.
options.note: The memorial is commanded by the LORD for Israel's remembrance, not for Pharaoh's benefit.

options.text: So Israel could forget what happened in Egypt.
options.note: The opposite is true; the feast exists precisely so Israel would never forget.

options.text: There is no stated reason for keeping it.
options.note: The text gives an explicit reason, remembering the exodus from Egypt.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament interpret the Passover lamb?

options.text: As a picture fulfilled in Christ, our Passover lamb, sacrificed once for all.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 5:7 states this directly, and John's Gospel echoes Passover details at the cross.

options.text: As a rite Christians are still commanded to repeat every year.
options.note: The New Testament treats it as fulfilled in Christ rather than an ongoing obligation for the church.

options.text: As a story with no connection to Jesus.
options.note: The connections, in Paul, John, and Peter, are explicit and deliberate.

options.text: As a purely political event with no theological meaning.
options.note: The New Testament treats it as deeply theological, the pattern for substitutionary atonement.

questions: The lamb had to be spotless, standing in for a household that was not. What does it mean for you that Christ, the truly spotless one, stood in your place?
The blood had to be applied, seen on the door, not just shed in the yard. Is your trust resting on Christ's finished work actually applied to you by faith, or on some vaguer hope?
Israel ate in haste, dressed for a journey that would begin that very night. Are you living each day as someone ready to be moved by God, or settled and comfortable in Egypt?
The feast was for remembering, told to children for generations. How well do you tell the story of your own rescue in Christ to the people who come after you?
The people bowed down and worshiped, then simply did what they were told. Where is God asking for that same combination from you this week, worship followed by obedience?

translationNotes.note: Twilight renders a Hebrew phrase literally meaning between the two evenings, understood as the late afternoon before sunset, the time appointed for the lambs to be slaughtered.
The LORD's Passover translates pesach, which can mean both the act of passing over in judgment and the festival meal itself; the wordplay is deliberate through the whole chapter.
Cut off from Israel likely describes exclusion from the covenant community, whether by formal expulsion or divine judgment; the severity underlines how seriously God takes this ordinance.
